readings.title: The Secret Garden: the child nobody wanted to see (Chapter I, first part)
readings.challenge: Separate what the narrator tells you about Mary from what you see her do, and decide who is to blame for the way she is.
readings.focus: The novel opens on an unloved, spoiled, sickly girl in India, and on a morning when something is plainly wrong.
readings.context: The Secret Garden (1911) is by Frances Hodgson Burnett, who was born in Manchester, England, moved to the United States as a girl, and wrote stories for a living from her teens. The text here is the first American edition, New York, August 1911. Mary Lennox is the daughter of an English official in India, which Britain then ruled as a colony; English families there kept many Indian servants. An Ayah is a nursemaid; “Mem Sahib” was the servants’ title for an English lady and “Missie Sahib” for an English girl; a governess is a teacher who lives with a family; a veranda is a roofed porch; hibiscus is a large tropical flower; “in a passion” means in a rage; going “to the hills” meant escaping the hot plains for cooler hill towns, where disease spread less; imploringly means begging.
readings.contentNote: Mary beats and kicks a servant and calls the Indian servants pigs; the narrator speaks of “the dark faces” of “native servants,” the colonial language of its time. A disease is spreading, and someone dies offstage.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “There Is No One Left,” from the opening through Mrs. Lennox running into the house; opens “When Mary Lennox was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle everybody said…”; closes “…the Mem Sahib cried. "Come with me! Come with me!" and she turned and ran into the house.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Mary’s face yellow, and how did her parents treat her as a baby?
facilitatorNotes: She was born in India and was always ill. Her father was busy and ill himself; her mother “cared only to go to parties,” did not want a girl, and told the Ayah to keep her “out of sight as much as possible.” So she was kept out of the way as a baby and as a toddler. The narrator is harsh about Mary’s looks, but shows the neglect behind them.
evidence: She had not wanted a little girl at all
she must keep the child out of sight as much as possible

questions.prompt: How did Mary become “as tyrannical and selfish a little pig as ever lived”? Is she to blame?
facilitatorNotes: The servants always gave her her own way, because the Mem Sahib would be angry if crying disturbed her; nobody ever told her no. Some readers will say a child cannot be blamed for how she was raised; others that she is still cruel, as when she beats the servant. Notice that the narrator calls Mary a “pig,” the very word Mary thinks the worst insult of all.
evidence: they always obeyed her and gave her her own way in everything
as tyrannical and selfish a little pig as ever lived

questions.prompt: What clues tell the reader that something is wrong that morning, before anyone says so?
facilitatorNotes: A strange servant comes instead of the Ayah, who “could not come”; nothing is done in its usual order; servants are missing, and the rest hurry about with “ashy and scared faces”; nobody tells Mary anything, and she is left alone; even her mother’s eyes are “large and scared.” The reader understands more than Mary, who only grows angrier.
evidence: There was something mysterious in the air that morning.
ashy and scared faces

questions.prompt: What does Mrs. Lennox say about the “silly dinner party”? What does her mistake show about her, and what do you predict?
facilitatorNotes: She should have left for the hills two weeks earlier but stayed for a party, and now calls herself a fool. The love of parties described in the first paragraph has put the whole household in danger. The wailing and “Some one has died” point toward disaster; ask readers what they expect for Mary.
evidence: I only stayed to go to that silly dinner party. What a fool I was!
You ought to have gone to the hills two weeks ago.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: There Is No One Left (Chapter I, end)
readings.challenge: Follow events that happen while Mary sleeps, and notice how the narrator lets us know more than she does.
readings.focus: Cholera empties the house; a forgotten child wakes alone and learns in a few words that her parents are dead.
readings.context: Recap: Mary Lennox, a sickly, spoiled and unloved nine-year-old English girl in India, woke to find her Ayah missing and the servants frightened; her mother, who had stayed for a dinner party instead of leaving for the hills, has just learned that someone in the household has died. Cholera is a disease spread by dirty water, which before modern medicine killed very quickly; a bungalow is a one-storey house; the compound is the fenced ground around it; desolation is emptiness and ruin; “kid” is slang for a child.
readings.contentNote: Cholera kills Mary’s Ayah, several servants and both her parents; the dead are carried away while she sleeps. Alone and thirsty, Mary drinks a glass of wine and falls into a heavy sleep.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “There Is No One Left,” from the cholera to the end of the chapter; opens “After that appalling things happened, and the mysteriousness of the morning was explained…”; closes “…was true that there was no one in the bungalow but herself and the little rustling snake.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mary do on the second day, and why does nobody find her?
facilitatorNotes: She hides in the nursery, cries and sleeps, eats fruit and biscuits from a half-finished meal, and drinks a glass of wine without knowing how strong it is, which sends her into a heavy sleep. Everyone is “too panic-stricken to think of a little girl no one was fond of.”
evidence: Nobody thought of her, nobody wanted her
Every one was too panic-stricken to think of a little girl no one was fond of.

questions.prompt: When she wakes in the silent house, what does Mary think about her Ayah’s death? What does that show?
facilitatorNotes: She does not cry; she wonders who will look after her now, and hopes a new Ayah will know new stories, since she was tired of the old ones. It is shocking, and the narrator says she “had never cared much for any one.” But no one had cared much for her either; readers may judge her, pity her, or both.
evidence: She did not cry because her nurse had died.
There would be a new Ayah, and perhaps she would know some new stories.

questions.prompt: The little snake appears in the nursery and again in the chapter’s last sentence. Why might Burnett bring it back?
facilitatorNotes: It is the only living thing that comes to her, and like everyone else it is in a hurry to leave. Mary is not afraid of it. The last sentence turns her own remark into the plain truth: there is no one in the house but her and the snake. Her loneliness becomes something we can see.
evidence: It sounds as if there was no one in the bungalow but me and the snake.
no one in the bungalow but herself and the little rustling snake

questions.prompt: How do Mary and the officers react to each other? Is her stiff reply rude, brave or something else?
facilitatorNotes: The officer is so startled he almost jumps back and calls the house “a place like this”; Mary draws herself up, offended, demands to know why nobody comes, and stamps her foot. She does not understand what has happened, and she is used to being obeyed. Barney seems to blink back tears. Readers may see rudeness, shock, or a child’s way of not being afraid. The chapter title answers her question.
evidence: the little girl said, drawing herself up stiffly
There is nobody left to come.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: Mistress Mary Quite Contrary (Chapter II, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice what Mary thinks, and does not think, about her parents, and compare how children and grown-ups talk about her.
readings.focus: At a clergyman’s crowded house Mary earns a nickname and hears of her unknown uncle, and the grown-ups judge her mother as well as her.
readings.context: Recap: cholera killed Mary’s parents and the servants in India, and officers found her alone in the empty bungalow. Now she is staying with an English clergyman’s family, the Crawfords, until she can be sent to England. A rockery is a garden of stones and plants; impudent means cheeky; scorn is contempt; desolate means lonely and empty. “Mistress Mary, quite contrary” is an old nursery rhyme; contrary means always wanting the opposite.
readings.contentNote: Basil calls Mary’s uncle “a hunchback” and “horrid,” mocking a man whose back is curved, and says girls never know anything. The grown-ups call Mary “plain” and unattractive.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,” from the opening through the Crawfords’ talk about Mary; opens “Mary had liked to look at her mother from a distance and she had thought her very pretty,…”; closes “…when he opened the door and found her standing by herself in the middle of the room."”.

questions.prompt: Does Mary miss her mother? How does the narrator explain it?
facilitatorNotes: Not at all. She had liked to look at her mother from a distance but knew very little of her, so she “could scarcely have been expected” to love her. The narrator half excuses Mary here. What she does think about is whether her new people will be polite and give her her own way.
evidence: She did not miss her at all, in fact
as she knew very little of her she could scarcely have been expected to love her

questions.prompt: What is Mary doing when Basil comes, and how does the teasing begin?
facilitatorNotes: She is making heaps of earth and paths for a garden, as on the day the cholera broke out. Basil becomes interested and suggests a rockery; she shouts “Go away! I don’t want boys.” His teasing answers her rudeness. Readers may blame Basil, Mary or both. Keep the garden in mind: it is the second time she has played at making one.
evidence: She was making heaps of earth and paths for a garden
Why don't you put a heap of stones there and pretend it is a rockery?

questions.prompt: What does Basil tell Mary about her uncle? Which parts sound like facts and which like gossip?
facilitatorNotes: He heard his parents say that she is going to her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, in England: that sounds like fact. That the house is desolate, that nobody goes near him, that he is “so cross” and “horrid” sounds like gossip, repeated with a seven-year-old’s nastiness (“Girls never do”). Mary stops her ears, but “thought over it a great deal afterward.”
evidence: I heard father and mother talking about him.
But she thought over it a great deal afterward

questions.prompt: What do the grown-ups say about Mary and her mother? Whom do they seem to blame?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Crawford calls Mary plain, with “the most unattractive ways,” and says one can understand the nickname. The reply blames Mrs. Lennox: if she had brought her pretty manners into the nursery more often, Mary might have learned some; Mrs. Crawford adds that she “scarcely ever looked at her.” Readers may ask whether it is fair to call a newly orphaned child plain at all.
evidence: Perhaps if her mother had carried her pretty face and her pretty manners oftener into the nursery
I believe she scarcely ever looked at her

readings.title: The Secret Garden: Mrs. Medlock (Chapter II, continued)
readings.challenge: Watch two people who dislike each other on sight, and find the new thought Mary has begun to have.
readings.focus: Mary reaches England, is collected by her uncle’s housekeeper, and for the first time wonders why she never belonged to anyone.
readings.context: Recap: orphaned in India, Mary stayed for a few days with a clergyman’s family, whose children called her “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary” and told her she would be sent to her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, in England. A mantle is a cloak; jet is shiny black stone used for beads; a bonnet is a hat tied under the chin; “a plain little piece of goods” is a rude way of saying plain; sallow means yellowish; a guardian is the person legally responsible for a child; crêpe is a crinkly cloth, and black clothes were worn for mourning; Yorkshire is a large county in the north of England.
readings.contentNote: The grown-ups talk in front of Mary about how plain she is.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,” from the voyage to England through Mrs. Medlock’s view of Mary on the train; opens “Mary made the long voyage to England under the care of an officer's wife, who was taking…”; closes “…and at last she got tired of watching her and began to talk in a brisk, hard voice.”.

questions.prompt: What do Mrs. Medlock and Mary each think of the other at first sight?
facilitatorNotes: Mrs. Medlock: “a plain little piece of goods.” Mary: “the most disagreeable person she had ever seen,” with a “common” face and a “common fine bonnet,” and she walks apart so that no one will think she belongs to her. Each judges the other by looks.
evidence: My word! she's a plain little piece of goods!
with her common, highly colored face and her common fine bonnet

questions.prompt: Mary seems not to be listening at the hotel window. What does she hear, and what does she wonder?
facilitatorNotes: She hears every word and becomes “very curious” about her uncle and his house, and wonders what a hunchback is, since she has never seen one. She hides her interest, which is a habit of hers.
evidence: but she heard quite well and was made very curious about her uncle
What was a hunchback?

questions.prompt: What new, “queer” thoughts has Mary begun to have? What does she still not know about herself?
facilitatorNotes: She wonders why she never seemed to belong to anyone: other children belonged to their parents, but she had only servants, food and clothes, and no one noticed her. She does not know that she is disagreeable; she sees it in other people but not in herself. This is the first sign that she may change.
evidence: she had never seemed to really be any one's little girl
She often thought that other people were, but she did not know that she was so herself.

questions.prompt: Why has Mrs. Medlock come for Mary, and what do Mr. Craven’s words show about him?
facilitatorNotes: She did not want to come, but she keeps her well-paid place by doing at once what he says, and she “never dared even to ask a question.” He speaks “in his short, cold way”: Mary is a duty he has as guardian, not a niece he wants. Readers can set this beside Mary’s new wish to belong to someone.
evidence: in his short, cold way
She never dared even to ask a question.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: a queer place (Chapter II, end)
readings.challenge: Notice when Mary pretends not to care, and when her interest slips out.
readings.focus: On the train Mrs. Medlock describes the huge, shut-up house and its lonely master, and Mary’s sympathy comes and goes.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Medlock, housekeeper to Mary’s uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, met Mary in London; now they are travelling north by train to his house in Yorkshire, and neither likes the other. Discomfited means made uneasy; a moor is high, wild, open land; involuntary means without meaning to; “Riquet à la Houppe” (Riquet with the Tuft) is a French fairy tale in which a clever, ugly prince wins a beautiful princess; the West Wing is one side of the house; frocks are dresses.
readings.contentNote: Mr. Craven is called a hunchback whose “crooked back” “set him wrong,” period language that links a disability with a sour character. His wife’s death is mentioned.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,” from Mrs. Medlock’s questions on the train to the end of the chapter; opens “"I suppose I may as well tell you something about where you are going to," she said. "Do…”; closes “…steadily that the grayness grew heavier and heavier before her eyes and she fell asleep.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mrs. Medlock tell Mary about the house? Which details make it sound strange?
facilitatorNotes: It is six hundred years old, on the edge of the moor, with nearly a hundred rooms, most of them shut up and locked; there are pictures and old furniture, a park, gardens and trees with trailing branches; then, suddenly, “But there’s nothing else.” The abrupt ending makes the grand house sound empty and sad.
evidence: there's near a hundred rooms in it, though most of them's shut up and locked
But there's nothing else,

questions.prompt: Mary answers “Nothing” and “It doesn’t matter … whether I care or not.” Does she care? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: She has “begun to listen in spite of herself,” her eyes turn toward Mrs. Medlock against her will, and she gives “a little involuntary jump” at the wife’s death. The narrator calls hiding her interest one of her “unhappy, disagreeable ways.” Mrs. Medlock says she is “like an old woman.”
evidence: Mary had begun to listen in spite of herself.
Mary gave a little involuntary jump.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary suddenly feel sorry for Mr. Craven, and why does the feeling stop?
facilitatorNotes: A fairy tale about a hunchback and a princess comes into her mind, and she is sorry he lost his wife. Then she hears that he cares about nobody and that she must not go poking about, and she decides he deserves what happened to him. Her sympathy depends on how he may treat her. Readers may call that selfish, or a lonely child protecting herself.
evidence: it had made her suddenly sorry for Mr. Archibald Craven
to think he was unpleasant enough to deserve all that had happened to him

questions.prompt: How does the rain at the end match Mary’s mood? What do Mrs. Medlock’s rules make you predict?
facilitatorNotes: The grey rain seems to go on “forever and ever,” like the dreary future she imagines, and she stares until she falls asleep. The rules (keep out of certain rooms, no “wandering and poking about,” though “There’s gardens enough”) are the kind a story usually breaks. Mary says she will not want to poke about; readers can predict whether she keeps her word.
evidence: the gray rain-storm which looked as if it would go on forever and ever
don't go wandering and poking about

readings.title: The Secret Garden: Thwaite Station (Chapter III, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow a journey in the dark through what Mary can glimpse, and notice how her upbringing shows in small actions.
readings.focus: After a long day on the train, Mary is driven from a little Yorkshire station into the dark, past the last lights of a village.
readings.context: The Secret Garden (1911) is by Frances Hodgson Burnett, who was born in Manchester, England, moved to the United States as a girl, and wrote stories for a living from her teens. The text here is the first American edition, New York, August 1911. Recap: after her parents died of cholera in India, nine-year-old Mary Lennox, a spoiled and lonely girl, was sent to England to her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, whom she has never met. His housekeeper, Mrs. Medlock, is taking her by train to his six-hundred-year-old house, Misselthwaite Manor, on the edge of a Yorkshire moor; she says most of its hundred rooms are locked and that Mr. Craven will not see Mary. Waterproofs are raincoats; the guard is the railwayman in charge of a train; a brougham (say “broom”) is a closed carriage; a footman is a servant in uniform; the box is the driver’s seat; a public house is a pub; a vicarage is a vicar’s house. The station-master speaks broad Yorkshire: “tha’s” is you have, “browt” brought, “th’ young ’un” the young one, “enow” enough.
readings.contentNote: Mary expects to be waited on because in India “native servants always picked up or carried things,” a colonial habit the narrator points out.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Across the Moor,” from the train through the carriage reaching the moor; opens “She slept a long time, and when she awakened Mrs. Medlock had bought a lunchbasket at one…”; closes “…forward and pressed her face against the window just as the carriage gave a big jolt.”.

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Medlock change after her tea? What does Mary watch her do?
facilitatorNotes: She cheers up, eats a great deal, and falls asleep, and Mary watches her fine bonnet slide to one side. The woman Mary thought so disagreeable looks ordinary and a little comic asleep.
evidence: Mrs. Medlock cheered up very much over her tea and chicken and beef
watched her fine bonnet slip on one side

questions.prompt: Why does Mary not offer to help with the parcels? What does the narrator want us to understand?
facilitatorNotes: In India servants always carried things, so it seems “quite proper” to her that others should wait on her. The narrator explains the habit without excusing it; it is the same upbringing we saw in Chapter I.
evidence: The little girl did not offer to help her
it seemed quite proper that other people should wait on one

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Medlock speak to the station-master? What does that show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She answers in a Yorkshire accent herself and asks after his wife: she is at home here, and friendlier than she has been with Mary. People can seem different in their own place.
evidence: speaking with a Yorkshire accent herself
How's thy Missus?

questions.prompt: Is Mary afraid on the drive? What does she see before the darkness begins?
facilitatorNotes: She is “not at all a timid child” and “not exactly frightened,” but feels there is “no knowing what might happen” in such a house. She sees cottages, a pub, a church and vicarage, a little shop with toys and sweets, then hedges and trees, then nothing but darkness, just as the carriage jolts. The familiar world falls away piece by piece. Readers can decide whether “not exactly frightened” means a little frightened.
evidence: she was not exactly frightened
She could see nothing, in fact, but a dense darkness on either side.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: Across the Moor (Chapter III, end)
readings.challenge: Picture a place you cannot see from its sounds, and gather the details that make a house feel unwelcoming.
readings.focus: Mary crosses the dark moor, which sounds like the sea, and arrives at a vast, dim house whose master will not see her.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Medlock and Mary left the train at little Thwaite Station in the rain and are driving at night in a closed carriage toward Misselthwaite Manor. Mary has just asked, “What is a moor?” Heather, gorse and broom are low wild shrubs; a lodge is a small house at the gate of an estate; the park is the land around a great house; an avenue is a road lined with trees; a vault is an arched roof, or a dark room under one; suits of armour were worn by knights; unceremoniously means without politeness.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Across the Moor,” from the carriage on the moor to the end of the chapter; opens “"Eh! We're on the moor now sure enough," said Mrs. Medlock.”; closes “…at Misselthwaite Manor and she had perhaps never felt quite so contrary in all her life.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mary think the moor is, and why?
facilitatorNotes: She asks whether it is the sea: the wind makes “a wild, low, rushing sound,” and the darkness spreads out on every side, so she feels she is crossing a black ocean on a strip of dry land. Mrs. Medlock explains: miles of wild land with heather, gorse and broom, and nothing living there but wild ponies and sheep.
evidence: It's--it's not the sea, is it?
a wide expanse of black ocean through which she was passing on a strip of dry land

questions.prompt: Mrs. Medlock finds the moor dreary but says “there’s plenty that likes it.” What does Mary decide? What might change her mind one day?
facilitatorNotes: “I don’t like it,” she tells herself twice, pinching her lips. Mrs. Medlock drops a hint that the moor looks different “when the heather’s in bloom.” Readers can predict whether Mary will always feel this way, and what would have to happen first.
evidence: particularly when the heather's in bloom
she pinched her thin lips more tightly together

questions.prompt: Find three details of the house and the hall that make Mary feel “small and lost and odd.”
facilitatorNotes: A long, low house rambling round a stone court with only one dim light upstairs; a huge oak door with iron nails and bars; a dim hall where the portraits and suits of armour seem to watch her; and Mary herself, “a very small, odd little black figure” on the stone floor. The two miles of dark avenue “like a long dark vault” prepare for it.
evidence: an immensely long but low-built house which seemed to ramble round a stone court
she felt as small and lost and odd as she looked

questions.prompt: What orders do Mr. Pitcher and Mrs. Medlock give? Why might the last sentence call her “Mistress Mary” again?
facilitatorNotes: Mr. Craven will not see her and leaves for London in the morning; he must not see “what he doesn’t want to see”; she must keep to her two rooms. The nickname from Chapter II returns: unwelcome again, she feels more contrary than ever. Readers may remember the rhyme’s question too, “How does your garden grow?”
evidence: he doesn't see what he doesn't want to see
she had perhaps never felt quite so contrary in all her life

readings.title: The Secret Garden: Martha (Chapter IV, first part)
readings.challenge: Compare how Mary and Martha each see the world, and notice where each is wrong.
readings.focus: On her first morning in Yorkshire, Mary meets a housemaid who talks to her as an equal; their quarrel ends with Mary sobbing with loneliness and Martha comforting her.
readings.context: The Secret Garden (1911) is by Frances Hodgson Burnett, who was born in Manchester, England, moved to the United States as a girl, and wrote stories for a living from her teens. The text here is the first American edition, New York, August 1911. Recap of Chapters I–III: Mary Lennox, a sickly, spoiled and bad-tempered girl of nine, grew up in India, where her British parents left her to Indian servants. When cholera killed her parents, she was sent to live with her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, at Misselthwaite Manor, a huge old house on the Yorkshire moors. A moor is wide, open, hilly land covered with heather; gorse and broom are shrubs with yellow flowers; an Ayah was an Indian nursemaid; a salaam is a low bow; imperious means bossy; a scullery-maid did the roughest kitchen work; blacking polished the iron grate. Martha speaks Yorkshire dialect: tha’ and thee mean you, thysen yourself, canna’ can’t, wi’ with, th’ the. Tracts were religious pamphlets, and “a man and a brother” comes from an old slogan against slavery.
readings.contentNote: Mary has slapped her Indian nurse; the narrator calls Indian servants servile; Martha uses the old word “blacks”; and Mary says Indian people “are not people.” These are the racist ideas of the British Empire in Burnett’s time. Mary calls Martha a “daughter of a pig.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Martha,” from Mary’s first morning at Misselthwaite through Martha comforting her; opens “When she opened her eyes in the morning it was because a young housemaid had come into…”; closes “…effect on Mary. She gradually ceased crying and became quiet. Martha looked relieved.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mary see from her window, and how do she and Martha each feel about it?
facilitatorNotes: A great bare stretch of land like “an endless, dull, purplish sea”: the moor. Mary hates it. Martha loves it: gorse, broom and heather in flower, the smell of honey, fresh air, bees and skylarks. The same view looks dead to one and alive to the other.
evidence: and to look rather like an endless, dull, purplish sea
It's covered wi' growin' things as smells sweet.

questions.prompt: How is Martha different from the servants Mary knew in India?
facilitatorNotes: She talks to Mary as an equal, laughs, and says what she thinks. In India Mary gave orders, never said please or thank you, and slapped her Ayah. Mary even wonders whether Martha might slap back. Notice that this is Mary’s view, and the narrator’s, of Indian servants, shaped by an empire that put British people above Indians.
evidence: Indian servants were commanded to do things, not asked.
she had a sturdy way which made Mistress Mary wonder if she might not even slap back

questions.prompt: Martha says she expected Mary to be black. Why does that make Mary so furious, and what do both girls get wrong?
facilitatorNotes: Mary has been taught that British people are above Indians, so to be taken for “a native” is an insult to her, and she says Indians “are not people.” That is racist and plainly wrong, and the story means Mary to grow out of it. Martha is curious and friendly, but she has never met a black person and lumps together everyone who is not white, from what she has read in tracts. Both girls show ignorance; only Mary shows contempt.
evidence: They are not people--they're servants who must salaam to you.
I've never seen a black an' I was fair pleased to think I was goin' to see one close.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary suddenly start sobbing, and what stops her?
facilitatorNotes: Behind the rage is loneliness: she feels “so horribly lonely and far away from everything she understood and which understood her.” Martha is frightened and sorry, begs her pardon, and her friendly Yorkshire way of talking comforts Mary. It is the first time anyone in the book has comforted her.
evidence: she suddenly felt so horribly lonely and far away from everything she understood
There was something comforting and really friendly in her queer Yorkshire speech

readings.title: The Secret Garden: “It was the custom” (Chapter IV, continued)
readings.challenge: Notice what Mary has never had to do, and what she has never had to go without.
readings.focus: Martha dresses Mary in new colourful clothes, tells her about her eleven brothers and sisters on the moor, and is shocked when Mary will not eat her porridge.
readings.context: Recap: On her first morning at Misselthwaite Manor, Mary met Martha, a cheerful Yorkshire housemaid who talks to her as an equal. They quarrelled, Mary burst into sobs of loneliness, and Martha comforted her. Mary has been wearing black because her parents have just died. To not “hold with” something is to disapprove of it; subservient means humbly obedient; a rustic is a country person; sixteen shillings a week was a very poor wage even then; treacle is syrup; victuals are food; pinafores are aprons.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Martha,” from Mary’s new clothes through the untouched porridge; opens “"It's time for thee to get up now," she said. "Mrs. Medlock said I was to carry tha'…”; closes “…same as th' rest. Then I go home an' clean up for mother an' give her a day's rest."”.

questions.prompt: Why has Mr. Craven ordered new clothes for Mary? What does it suggest about him?
facilitatorNotes: He will not have a child in black “wanderin' about like a lost soul,” making the house sadder. Though he is away and never sees her, he has thought about her, and about the sadness of the house.
evidence: I won't have a child dressed in black wanderin' about like a lost soul
Put color on her.

questions.prompt: “It was the custom.” What does Mary mean, and what does dressing teach both girls?
facilitatorNotes: In India her Ayah always dressed her, so she stands and holds out her foot. Martha, who has buttoned up her little brothers and sisters, has never seen a child wait “as if she had neither hands nor feet of her own.” Mary begins to suspect that Misselthwaite will teach her to do things for herself.
evidence: as if she had neither hands nor feet of her own
her life at Misselthwaite Manor would end by teaching her a number of things quite new to her

questions.prompt: What makes Mary feel “a slight interest” in Dickon? Why is that called a “healthy sentiment”?
facilitatorNotes: Dickon found a wild pony on the moor and made friends with it, and Mary has always wanted a pet. It is the first time she has been interested in anyone except herself, the first sign that she can grow.
evidence: Dickon's a kind lad an' animals likes him.
as she had never before been interested in any one but herself, it was the dawning of a healthy sentiment

questions.prompt: “I don't know what it is to be hungry.” Why does this make Martha indignant?
facilitatorNotes: Martha’s twelve brothers and sisters live on sixteen shillings a week and have “scarce ever” had full stomachs. Mary says it with “the indifference of ignorance”: she has never had to think about others. Martha will not take the food home either, because it is not hers. Readers may talk about what each girl knows that the other does not.
evidence: Because they scarce ever had their stomachs full in their lives.
said Mary, with the indifference of ignorance

readings.title: The Secret Garden: the garden no one has seen (Chapter IV, continued)
readings.challenge: Follow Mary’s first search for the locked garden, and notice what draws her on.
readings.focus: Martha tells Mary about a garden that has been locked for ten years, and Mary searches the walled gardens until a robin sings to her from beyond a wall with no door.
readings.context: Recap: Mary is learning that at Misselthwaite she will have to do things for herself. Martha, the housemaid, chatters about her eleven brothers and sisters on the moor, especially Dickon, twelve, who makes friends with wild animals. Mary would not eat her porridge. A shrubbery is a mass of bushes; kitchen-gardens grow vegetables and fruit; fruit-trees “trained flat against the wall” are grown flat on the warm bricks; glass frames are low glass covers for young plants; surly means bad-tempered; nowt means nothing.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Martha,” from Martha sending Mary outdoors through the robin’s song in the orchard; opens “Mary drank some tea and ate a little toast and some marmalade.”; closes “…into his winter song--almost as if he had caught sight of her and was calling to her.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary decide to go outside?
facilitatorNotes: There is nothing to do indoors, and Martha says she must learn to play alone. But the narrator says it was really the mention of Dickon and his birds, “though she was not aware of it.” Something new is pulling at her.
evidence: It was really this mention of Dickon which made Mary decide to go out, though she was not aware of it.

questions.prompt: What does Martha tell Mary about the locked garden? Why might she hesitate before saying it?
facilitatorNotes: Mr. Craven locked it when his wife died suddenly, dug a hole and buried the key, and no one has been in for ten years. Martha may hesitate because it is a sad subject in the house, or because she is not supposed to talk about it. Then the bell saves her.
evidence: One of th' gardens is locked up. No one has been in it for ten years.
He locked th' door an' dug a hole and buried th' key.

questions.prompt: “How could a garden be shut up? You could always walk into a garden.” How does Mary search, and what does she find?
facilitatorNotes: She goes through the shrubbery and the bare formal gardens to a series of walled kitchen-gardens, trying every green door; the last leads to an orchard. The wall runs on beyond it, with treetops showing above, but there is no door anywhere.
evidence: How could a garden be shut up? You could always walk into a garden.
but there was no green door to be seen anywhere

questions.prompt: Why does this part end with the robin? What might he have to do with the garden?
facilitatorNotes: He sits on a treetop beyond the wall, where the locked garden ought to be, and bursts into song “almost as if he had caught sight of her and was calling to her.” He seems to belong to the garden and to be inviting her in. Readers can predict what he will do.
evidence: She could see the tops of trees above the wall
almost as if he had caught sight of her and was calling to her

readings.title: The Secret Garden: the robin and Ben Weatherstaff (Chapter IV, continued)
readings.challenge: Watch how a bird changes two sour people, and notice the moment Mary learns something about herself.
readings.focus: A surly old gardener whistles down his friend the robin, tells how it was once a lonely fledgling, and Mary realises that she is lonely too.
readings.context: Recap: Martha told Mary about a garden locked for ten years: Mr. Craven shut it and buried the key when his wife died suddenly. Exploring the walled kitchen-gardens and the orchard, Mary found no door into it, but she saw treetops beyond the wall, and a red-breasted bird singing on one. Desolate means lonely and miserable; crustily means grumpily; “forrad” means forward, too bold; a fledgling is a young bird just learning to fly; a brood is a family of young birds; “Mester” is Mister; meddlin’ is interfering.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Martha,” from Mary listening to the robin through “I’m lonely”; opens “She stopped and listened to him and somehow his cheerful, friendly little whistle gave…”; closes “…She seemed to find it out when the robin looked at her and she looked at the robin.”.

questions.prompt: How does the robin’s song make Mary feel, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Pleased, almost smiling. The big closed house, the bare moor and the bare gardens have made her feel “as if there was no one left in the world but herself,” and the friendly little whistle breaks into that. The narrator says even a disagreeable child can be lonely.
evidence: even a disagreeable little girl may be lonely
the bright-breasted little bird brought a look into her sour little face which was almost a smile

questions.prompt: What changes in Ben Weatherstaff when Mary mentions the bird?
facilitatorNotes: His surly face breaks into a slow smile, and he whistles a soft, coaxing whistle she would never have expected from him. Mary notices for the first time “how much nicer a person looked when he smiled.”
evidence: It made her think that it was curious how much nicer a person looked when he smiled.
She could not understand how such a surly man could make such a coaxing sound.

questions.prompt: How does Ben talk about the robin? What does that show about Ben?
facilitatorNotes: Like a person, or a child: a cheeky beggar, conceited, curious, “th' head gardener.” He knows the bird’s whole history. Under his gruffness he is proud of the robin and fond of him.
evidence: He looked at the plump little scarlet-waistcoated bird as if he were both proud and fond of him.
He's th' head gardener, he is.

questions.prompt: “I'm lonely.” Why does Mary discover this only now?
facilitatorNotes: Ben tells how the robin’s brood was scattered and “he knew he was lonely,” so he came back to the gardener. Looking at the robin, Mary recognises herself, and finds out that loneliness is part of what has made her sour and cross. Naming a feeling is the first step to changing it.
evidence: This one was a knowin' one an' he knew he was lonely.
She had not known before that this was one of the things which made her feel sour and cross.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: no door (Chapter IV, end)
readings.challenge: Notice how plain speaking affects Mary, and why the old gardener turns rough at the end.
readings.focus: Ben Weatherstaff tells Mary the blunt truth about herself, the robin chooses to make friends with her, and Ben refuses to talk about the door to the hidden garden.
readings.context: Recap: In the kitchen-garden Mary met Ben Weatherstaff, a surly old gardener, whose face changed when he whistled down his friend the robin. The robin had come out of the locked garden as a lonely fledgling. Watching him, Mary said for the first time, “I’m lonely.” A wench is a girl; “wove out of th' same cloth” means made the same way; “I'll warrant” means I’m sure; frankness is honesty; to take a fancy to is to like; meddlesome means interfering; uncompanionable means unfriendly.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Martha,” from Ben Weatherstaff’s questions to the end of the chapter; opens “The old gardener pushed his cap back on his bald head and stared at her a minute.”; closes “…spade over his shoulder and walked off, without even glancing at her or saying good-by.”.

questions.prompt: Ben says he and Mary are “wove out of th' same cloth.” What does he mean, and how does Mary take it?
facilitatorNotes: Both plain-looking, both sour, both bad-tempered, and both lonely. Mary has never heard the truth about herself; servants always bowed to her. She does not snap back: she wonders whether he is right, and feels uncomfortable, which is a beginning.
evidence: We're neither of us good lookin' an' we're both of us as sour as we look.
Mary Lennox had never heard the truth about herself in her life.

questions.prompt: How does Mary speak to the robin, and why is Ben surprised?
facilitatorNotes: Softly, eagerly, coaxingly, as if to a person: not in her hard voice or her bossy Indian voice. Ben says she sounded like “a real child instead of a sharp old woman,” like Dickon with his wild things. A gentler Mary is showing through.
evidence: in a tone so soft and eager and coaxing
tha' said that as nice an' human as if tha' was a real child instead of a sharp old woman

questions.prompt: What does Ben say about Dickon? How is Dickon becoming important before we meet him?
facilitatorNotes: Everybody knows him; even the blackberries and heather know him; foxes show him their cubs and skylarks do not hide their nests from him. This is the third time someone has spoken of Dickon’s way with animals, and Mary is now as curious about him as about the garden.
evidence: Th' very blackberries an' heather-bells knows him.
I warrant th' foxes shows him where their cubs lies

questions.prompt: Why does Ben suddenly turn rough when Mary asks about the door?
facilitatorNotes: He admits there were rose-trees ten years ago, then shuts the subject: there is no door now, “none as is any one's business,” and she must not meddle. Perhaps he is loyal to Mr. Craven, or the memory hurts, or he knows more than he says. His roughness only makes Mary, and the reader, more curious.
evidence: There was ten year' ago, but there isn't now
Don't you be a meddlesome wench an' poke your nose where it's no cause to go.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: the robin on the wall (Chapter V, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice the changes in Mary that she does not notice herself, and follow her reasoning about the door.
readings.focus: Days in the moor wind make Mary hungry and stronger; the robin greets her from a long ivy-covered wall, and she becomes sure the locked garden lies behind it.
readings.context: The Secret Garden (1911) is by Frances Hodgson Burnett, who was born in Manchester, England, moved to the United States as a girl, and wrote stories for a living from her teens. The text here is the first American edition, New York, August 1911. Recap of Chapter IV: Mary Lennox, a spoiled, sour orphan of nine sent from India to her uncle’s great house on the Yorkshire moors, has met Martha, a chatty Yorkshire housemaid, and Ben Weatherstaff, a surly old gardener whose friend is a robin. Martha told her of a garden that Mr. Craven locked ten years ago, burying the key, when his wife died; Mary found its walls, but no door. An avenue is a tree-lined drive; disdainfully means scornfully; victuals are food; sallow means sickly yellow; to preen is to tidy feathers; languid means listless.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Cry in the Corridor,” from Mary’s first days out of doors through her search for the door; opens “At first each day which passed by for Mary Lennox was exactly like the others. Every…”; closes “…moor had begun to blow the cobwebs out of her young brain and to waken her up a little.”.

questions.prompt: What is the wind doing for Mary that she does not know about?
facilitatorNotes: She runs only to keep warm and hates the wind, but it is stirring her “slow blood,” filling her lungs, putting colour in her cheeks and brightening her eyes. After a few days she wakes up hungry for the first time and empties her porridge bowl.
evidence: she was stirring her slow blood and making herself stronger by fighting with the wind
she wakened one morning knowing what it was to be hungry

questions.prompt: Mary says she does not play. What does she do instead, and what does she notice?
facilitatorNotes: She “looked at things,” walking the gardens day after day. At the lower end of one long walk the ivy on the wall is thick and untrimmed, as if that part had been left alone for years: a clue, though she does not yet know it.
evidence: Mary did not shout, but she looked at things.
There was one part of the wall where the creeping dark green leaves were more bushy than elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What does Mary imagine the robin says, and how does she answer? What happens to her face?
facilitatorNotes: “Good morning! Isn't the wind nice? … Come on! Come on!” She laughs, runs after him, tries to whistle and cries “I like you!”, and for a moment “thin, sallow, ugly Mary” looks almost pretty. Joy changes her looks as the smile changed Ben’s.
evidence: Isn't the wind nice? Isn't the sun nice? Isn't everything nice?
she actually looked almost pretty for a moment

questions.prompt: Follow Mary’s reasoning about the door. Why is she now “not sorry that she had come”?
facilitatorNotes: She sees the same treetop from the orchard and from the walk outside, so the garden lies between; there is no door on any side; but Mr. Craven buried a key, so there must once have been a door. The puzzle wakes her up: in India she was too hot and languid to care about anything.
evidence: But there must have been one ten years ago, because Mr. Craven buried the key.
the fresh wind from the moor had begun to blow the cobwebs out of her young brain

readings.title: The Secret Garden: wutherin’ (Chapter V, end)
readings.challenge: Listen with Mary to the sounds of a stormy night, and decide whom to believe about the last one.
readings.focus: By the fire on a windy night Martha tells why Mr. Craven hates the garden, and then Mary hears a child crying somewhere inside the house.
readings.context: Recap: Days out of doors in the moor wind have made Mary hungry and stronger. The robin greeted her from the top of a long ivy-covered wall, and she is sure he lives in the locked garden, but she can find no door. The servants’ hall is where the servants eat and sit; a footman is a manservant; a novelty is something new; “wutherin’” is a Yorkshire word for the wind’s roar; buffeting is battering; a draft is a draught of air; a scullery-maid does the roughest kitchen work.
readings.contentNote: Martha tells how Mrs. Craven fell when a branch broke in her garden and died the next day. Martha’s old word “blacks” for Indian servants appears again.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Cry in the Corridor,” from Mary’s question to Martha by the fire to the end of the chapter; opens “She stayed out of doors nearly all day, and when she sat down to her supper at night she…”; closes “…Mistress Mary stare very hard at her. She did not believe she was speaking the truth.”.

questions.prompt: What does “wutherin'” mean, and how does Mary work it out? Why does the storm make her feel safe?
facilitatorNotes: She listens until she understands: a hollow, shuddering roar going round and round the house, like an invisible giant beating at the walls to get in. Because he cannot get in, the room with its red coal fire feels all the safer and warmer.
evidence: It must mean that hollow shuddering sort of roar
somehow it made one feel very safe and warm inside a room with a red coal fire

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Craven hate the garden?
facilitatorNotes: It was his wife’s, made when they married; the two of them tended it alone and spent hours there. She liked to sit on an old bent branch she had grown roses over; it broke, she fell, and she died the next day. He nearly died of grief, and no one may go in or speak of it.
evidence: It was Mrs. Craven's garden that she had made when first they were married an' she just loved it
That's why he hates it.

questions.prompt: The narrator lists four good things that have happened to Mary. Which do you think matters most, and why?
facilitatorNotes: She felt she understood a robin; she ran in the wind until her blood was warm; she was healthily hungry; and she found out “what it was to be sorry for some one.” The last is new: until now she has thought only of herself. Readers may choose another and give a reason.
evidence: She had felt as if she had understood a robin and that he had understood her
she had found out what it was to be sorry for some one

questions.prompt: Who does Mary think is crying, and why doesn’t she believe Martha?
facilitatorNotes: Not the wind: the sound is inside the house, down a corridor, and when a door blows open it is clearer, a child’s cry, not a grown-up’s. Martha first says it is the wind, then a scullery-maid with toothache, and her manner is “troubled and awkward.” Two different excuses, and an uneasy face, make Mary sure she is hiding something.
evidence: It is some one crying--and it isn't a grown-up person.
She did not believe she was speaking the truth.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: a hundred closed doors (Chapter VI, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how Mary is changing, and what she is looking for as she explores the empty house.
readings.focus: On a rainy day Martha tells of Dickon’s rescued animals, and Mary, whom nobody watches, sets off alone to explore the hundred rooms of Misselthwaite Manor.
readings.context: Recap: Martha told Mary why the garden is locked: Mrs. Craven loved it, and died after a branch she sat on broke; Mr. Craven has hated it since. That night Mary heard a child crying somewhere inside the house; Martha said it was the wind, or a scullery-maid with toothache, but Mary did not believe her. Moithered means bothered; the bosom of a shirt is its front; a litter is a family of baby animals; “familiar” talk is talk that is too friendly; below stairs means in the servants’ part of the house; pewter is a grey metal for plates and mugs; “fair soft in th' head” means silly; authority is the right to give orders; a gallery is a long room for pictures; brocade is rich patterned cloth; ruffs are stiff frilled collars.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “There Was Some One Crying—There Was!”, from the rainy morning through Mary’s wandering in the portrait gallery; opens “The next day the rain poured down in torrents again, and when Mary looked out of her…”; closes “…have lived in them, but it all seemed so empty that she could not quite believe it true.”.

questions.prompt: What animals has Dickon rescued, and what do they tell you about him?
facilitatorNotes: A fox cub half drowned in its flooded hole after its mother was killed, and a young crow, now called Soot. He goes out even in the rain, because he “sees things on rainy days as doesn't show when it's fair weather.” He notices, and he cares.
evidence: He once found a little fox cub half drowned in its hole
He says he sees things on rainy days as doesn't show when it's fair weather.

questions.prompt: How has Mary changed toward Martha’s talk? Whom in Martha’s stories does she like best?
facilitatorNotes: She has forgotten to resent it, finds it interesting and is sorry when Martha stops. She is drawn most to Martha’s mother and Dickon: the stories about mother always sound “comfortable,” a word that tells what Mary has never had.
evidence: The time had come when Mary had forgotten to resent Martha's familiar talk.
Mary was most attracted by the mother and Dickon.

questions.prompt: “No one troubled themselves about her in the least.” What is good and what is bad about how Mary is treated at Misselthwaite?
facilitatorNotes: Bad: she is lonely and neglected; nobody asks what she does. Good: she is free, and she is learning to dress herself because Martha thinks her silly when she waits to be dressed. Martha’s remark about her four-year-old sister stung, but “made her think several entirely new things.” Readers can weigh which matters more.
evidence: no one troubled themselves about her in the least
it made her think several entirely new things

questions.prompt: Why does Mary speak to the portrait of the little girl with the green parrot?
facilitatorNotes: The girl is stiff and plain, “rather like herself,” with sharp, curious eyes. In the huge empty house Mary longs for a companion, and the painted girl is the nearest thing: “I wish you were here.” Like the other portrait children, she is long gone, which makes the wish sadder.
evidence: There was a stiff, plain little girl rather like herself.
I wish you were here.

readings.title: The Secret Garden: “There was some one crying” (Chapter VI, end)
readings.challenge: Collect what Mary finds behind the closed doors, and decide what the grown-ups are hiding.
readings.focus: Mary finds a girl’s portrait, a cabinet of ivory elephants and a nest of mice, hears the crying again, and is dragged back to her room by an angry Mrs. Medlock.
readings.context: Recap: On a rainy day, with no one caring what she did, Mary set out to explore the hundred rooms of Misselthwaite Manor. She wandered empty corridors and a gallery of old portraits, and spoke to a painting of a plain little girl holding a green parrot. Leaded panes are small window panes held in strips of lead; a mantel is the shelf over a fireplace; ivory is elephant tusk; a mahout is an elephant’s driver and a palanquin a covered seat; fretful means whining; to box someone’s ears is to hit them on the side of the head; a governess taught children at home.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “There Was Some One Crying—There Was!”, from the first door that opens to the end of the chapter; opens “It was not until she climbed to the second floor that she thought of turning the handle…”; closes “…elephants and had seen the gray mouse and its babies in their nest in the velvet cushion.”.

questions.prompt: What does Mary find behind the first door that opens?
facilitatorNotes: A big bedroom with embroidered hangings, furniture like the inlaid furniture of India, a window over the moor, and another portrait of the plain little girl, staring more curiously than ever. “She makes me feel queer,” says Mary.
evidence: over the mantel was another portrait of the stiff, plain little girl
She stares at me so that she makes me feel queer.

questions.prompt: Why do the ivory elephants and the mouse family matter to Mary?
facilitatorNotes: The elephants are something from India that she knows about; she plays with them a long time, then puts them back in order. The mice are the first living things in all the empty rooms: “seven mice who did not look lonely at all,” unlike Mary. She would like to take them home, a new wish for her.
evidence: Mary had seen carved ivory in India and she knew all about elephants.
there were seven mice who did not look lonely at all

questions.prompt: What happens when Mary hears the crying again?
facilitatorNotes: Lost in a short passage, she hears a fretful, childish whine, nearer than before. Touching the tapestry, she finds it covers a door, and Mrs. Medlock comes through with her keys, drags her back to her room, tells her she heard nothing, and threatens to box her ears and lock her up.
evidence: The tapestry was the covering of a door
You didn't hear anything of the sort

questions.prompt: Why might Mrs. Medlock deny the crying? What do you think is going on?
facilitatorNotes: Martha and Mrs. Medlock both deny it, and Mrs. Medlock is angry rather than puzzled, so something in the house is being kept secret. Mary, pale with rage, insists to herself, “There was some one crying,” and decides she will find out. Readers can predict whose cry it is and why it is hidden.
evidence: There _was_ some one crying--there _was_--there _was_!
She had heard it twice now, and sometime she would find out.
